name: wild
title: Backcountry
tagline: When the trail stops making sense
notice: General outdoor safety guidance. Conditions vary, so follow local park and rescue advice.

lost.title: Lost on the trail
steps: Stop walking. Sit down, drink water and calm your breathing.
Think: when did you last know where you were?
Look for landmarks, trail markers and your own footprints.
If you cannot retrace your route with confidence, stay where you are.
Make yourself visible and wait: searchers start from your last known point.
lost.urgent: Call 911 if you have signal. Moving in the dark or in bad weather makes rescue harder.

hypothermia.title: Hypothermia
steps: Get them out of wind and rain.
Replace wet clothes with dry layers and cover the head.
Wrap them in a sleeping bag or blankets and insulate them from the ground.
Give warm sweet drinks if they are awake.
Warm the chest and neck first, not the arms and legs.
hypothermia.urgent: Call for rescue if shivering stops, speech slurs or they become drowsy. Handle them gently.

water.title: Make water safe to drink
steps: Collect from moving water, upstream of camps and animals.
Strain out grit through a cloth.
Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m.
No stove: use a filter or purification tablets and wait the time on the label.
water.urgent: Clear water can still carry giardia. Untreated water is a last resort only when dehydration is the bigger danger.

bear.title: Black bear encounter
steps: Stay calm and do not run.
Speak in a low steady voice and back away slowly.
Make yourself look big and keep your group together.
Have bear spray ready and use it if the bear comes within about 5 m.
If a black bear attacks, fight back. Do not play dead.
bear.urgent: Never get between a bear and its cubs or food. Leave the area the way you came.

lightning.title: Caught in a thunderstorm
steps: Get off peaks, ridges and open ground right away.
Stay away from lone trees, water and metal fences.
Spread your group out, 15 m apart.
Crouch low on your pack with feet together if strikes are close.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before moving on.
lightning.urgent: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck.

night.title: Unplanned night out
steps: Stop while there is still light to work with.
Pick a spot out of the wind, away from water and dead branches.
Put on every layer and sit on your pack or a bed of branches.
Build a windbreak from branches, a tarp or an emergency blanket.
Eat something and stay together for warmth.
night.urgent: Cold ground takes heat faster than cold air. Insulate underneath you first.

signal.title: Signal for rescue
steps: Try 911 even with no bars, and text if calls fail.
Move to an open clearing or high ground.
Signal in threes: three whistle blasts, three flashes or three fires.
Lay out bright clothing or gear in a large X.
Stay put once you have signalled.
signal.urgent: Save phone battery: airplane mode between attempts, and keep the phone warm.

tick.title: Tick bite
steps: Grip the tick with fine tweezers as close to the skin as you can.
Pull straight out, slowly and steadily. Do not twist or squeeze the body.
Wash the bite and your hands with soap and water.
Note the date and keep the tick in a sealed bag.
Watch for a spreading rash or fever over the next 30 days.
tick.urgent: See a doctor if a bullseye rash, fever or joint pain appears: these can be signs of Lyme disease.

frostbite.title: Frostbite
steps: Get out of the cold and remove wet gloves, socks and rings.
Warm the area against warm skin, such as an armpit.
If you can stay warm afterward, soak in warm, not hot, water for 20 to 30 minutes.
Do not rub the skin or use snow.
Do not rewarm if it might freeze again before you reach help.
frostbite.urgent: White, hard or numb skin that stays that way needs medical care.

fire.title: Campfire safety
steps: Check the local fire ban before lighting anything.
Use an existing fire ring on bare ground, 3 m from tents and trees.
Keep it small and never leave it alone.
To put it out: drown with water, stir the ashes, drown again.
It is out when you can hold your hand in the ashes.
fire.urgent: If a fire escapes and you cannot stop it in seconds, leave and call 911.

examples: I am lost in the woods what do I do
my friend is shivering hard and slurring words in the cold
can I drink water from a stream
there is a bear on the trail
